items.definition: The overall security policy, run as a repeating Plan-Do-Check-Act cycle (ISO 27001).
items.examples: Reviewing and improving security measures every quarter.
items.examTip: PDCA = continuous improvement. Security is never finished because threats change.
keyFacts: Plan-Do-Check-Act loop from ISO 27001, so security keeps improving rather than standing still
Security as a repeating cycle, because threats change and the policy must keep up
Covers internet use, passwords, staff duties and training, so every area has clear rules

items.definition: Rules for acceptable internet and email use at work.
items.examples: Banning downloads of executable files; warning that email may be monitored.
items.examTip: Covers offensive material, confidential info, copyright, risky sites and monitoring.
keyFacts: No offensive or illegal material, which protects staff and the organisation's reputation
Rules on sending confidential information, so data isn't leaked by email
No copyrighted or risky downloads, which avoids malware and legal action
The organisation may scan traffic and keep emails, so staff know they can be monitored

items.definition: Rules and tools that enforce strong passwords and safe account use.
items.examples: Blocking common passwords; locking accounts after failed logins.
items.examTip: Include: length/strength, no sharing, no reuse, lockout, minimum age, expiry.
keyFacts: Length and strength rules make passwords harder to crack
A deny list of common passwords stops easily guessed choices like 'Password1'
Log attempts and lock out, so brute-force attacks are stopped and noticed
Use technology (e.g. MFA, password managers) to rely less on passwords alone

items.definition: What staff must do for security, and how they are trained.
items.examples: Annual security training; reporting suspicious emails.
items.examTip: Good training is funded, flexible, varied, tracked, rewarding and ongoing.
keyFacts: Staff must train, follow procedures and report suspicious activity, so threats are caught early
Training is ongoing and flexible, so it fits around work and keeps up with threats
Incentives, not punishment, so staff report mistakes instead of hiding them
Refreshed for new threats, because attackers keep changing their methods

items.definition: A check that the organisation follows its own security policies and the law.
items.examples: Finding accounts that still belong to ex-employees.
items.examTip: Finds gaps and checks against internal policy AND external law.
keyFacts: Set goals and scope, so the audit checks the right systems and areas
Find gaps and weaknesses before attackers do
Check against policy and law, so the organisation knows it is compliant
Report required improvements, so managers know what to fix and in what order

items.definition: A written policy stating what is backed up, how, how often and by whom.
items.examples: Nightly incrementals, weekly fulls, quarterly restore tests.
items.examTip: A good policy includes testing restores and legal compliance.
keyFacts: Sets which data, method and type (full, incremental, differential), so everything important is covered
Sets how often and where copies are stored, so recent data survives a site disaster
Names who is responsible, so backups aren't skipped or forgotten
Test backups regularly, so they are known to restore when needed

items.definition: A policy making sure the organisation follows data protection law (GDPR).
items.examples: Appointing a Data Protection Officer; covering contractors too.
items.examTip: Links to GDPR. Key parts: DPO, principles, rights, training, accountability.
keyFacts: Appoint a Data Protection Officer, so one person oversees GDPR compliance
Follow GDPR principles and rights, so personal data is handled lawfully
Train staff, so everyone knows how to handle personal data correctly
Applies to contractors too, because they may also handle the organisation's data

items.definition: The plan for how the organisation responds to a security incident.
items.examples: A triage flowchart and contact list including legal, PR, HR and insurance.
items.examTip: Stages: triage/escalate → contain, mitigate, recover → review and close.
keyFacts: Contacts list (response lead, IT, management, legal, PR, HR, insurance), so the right people act fast
Triage and escalation rate the incident's severity, so serious ones reach senior staff quickly
Contain, mitigate, recover: stop the spread, reduce the damage, then restore normal service
Review, report and close, so lessons are learned and the plan is improved

items.definition: A policy for restoring systems and operations after a major disruption.
items.examples: Deciding whether to trigger incident response, business continuity or full recovery.
items.examTip: Includes triage (rating severity), roles, contact lists and monitoring.
keyFacts: Clear purpose and scope, so everyone knows what the plan covers
Triage lists possible events and rates their severity, so the response matches the disaster
Choose which plan to activate, so staff follow the right steps for that event
Clear roles and contacts, so no time is wasted working out who does what

items.definition: A policy for using outside providers for cloud, hardware, software and support.
items.examples: A service level agreement setting response and fix times.
items.examTip: Covers authorisation, accountability, SLAs and incident handling.
keyFacts: Who authorises and who is accountable, so outside services aren't taken on without approval
Cloud: what's protected and how data protection is met, so GDPR still applies to data held by others
Vendors, licences and support agreements are recorded, so the organisation knows what it relies on
SLAs set response and fix times, so the provider can be held to account if service fails
